extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets
extraction.description: A dataset of millions of tiny colour images collected from the web, with labeled subsets CIFAR-10 (10 classes, 6000 images each) and CIFAR-100 (100 classes, 600 images each) for object recognition experiments.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky, with contributions from colleagues at MIT and NYU
extraction.citeAs: Leaming Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images, Alex Krizhevsky, April 8, 2009
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset was assembled by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet. Several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista were used, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting all the images for a particular search term, perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images collected from the web using search engines (Google, Flickr, Altavista) based on WordNet nouns.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Over the span of six months
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32. For the labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), duplicate images were removed by comparing with L2 norm and using a rejection threshold.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For unsupervised learning experiments, a subset of about 2 million images was used. Whitening transformation (ZCA) was applied to remove second-order correlations. In some experiments, the 1000 least significant principal components were deleted to reduce noise. Images were also segmented into patches (e.g., 8x8) for some training.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Labelers were given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, including hyponyms. They rejected images not belonging to the class based on criteria: class name should be high on the list of likely answers, image should be photo-realistic (no line drawings), contain only one prominent instance of the object, and object identity should be clear even if partially occluded or from an unusual viewpoint. Every label was personally verified by the authors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Duplicate images were removed from the labeled dataset by comparing with L2 norm and using a rejection threshold. The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with training set receiving 5000 randomly-selected images from each class for CIFAR-10.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, but it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has no reliable class labels originally, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) are limited to specific classes and may not generalize to all object types.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Unsupervised training of deep generative models, object recognition experiments (using labeled subsets CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), pre-training features for classifiers.
